previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy and GJ tube dependence, and a history of osteonecrosis was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He was found to have C. difficile infection and septic shock, with worsening respiratory status requiring ICU admission and temporary ventilation. A bronchoscopy revealed multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas and Klebsiella pneumonia, leading to treatment with meropenem and vancomycin. His condition improved over ten days with antibiotic therapy, weaning from support, and stabilization of vital signs. He was discharged to his extended care facility on IV antibiotics with plans for follow-up care.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ with HIV/AIDS on HAART s/p multiple complications of AIDS, 
recurrent c diff infections, chronic trach/PEG who presents with 
fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and positive UA.

#FEVER: initially presented with positive SIRS criteria, which 
resolved with fluid resuscitation and acetaminophen. Significant 
respiratory history including multiple episodes of PJP 
pneumonia, CMV/HSV pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial 
pneumonia. CXR on admission not overly suspicious for acute 
infectious process with actual interval improvement compared to 
prior. He did have ?aspiration event the day prior to admission 
- could have possibly caused aspiration pneumonitis vs 
pneumonia. Also low risk for CNS source given baseline mentation 
and unimpressed neurologic exam. 
He was initially in the ICU on broad spectrum antibiotics, but 
then transferred to the medicine floor and was seen by the ID 
service.  Given history suggestive of aspiration pneumonitis, 
antibiotics were stopped, and his fevers, tachycardia resolved.  
He was observed for nearly 72 hours off antibiotics and remained 
stable and afebrile throughout.  

#HYPERNATREMIA: The patient was hypernatremic to 152 on 
admission with prior normal sodium levels. Most likely this was 
felt to be due to inadequate free water through G tube, which 
may also explain why pt was found drinking water (despite being 
NPO) at SNF. Other possible etiology includes diabetes 
insipidus, especially in setting of prior CNS disease, although 
unlikely given concentrated urine sample obtained for U/A (spec 
___ of 1.028), which is inconsistent with DI. He was started on 
free water flushes through his ___ to address this issue with 
normalization of sodium levels.

#RECURRENT C DIFF:   C diff checked as he had diarrhea within a 
few days of antibiotics and testing was positive.  Result 
discussed with ID who advised long taper given that this is the 
fourth recurrence of his disease.  
Taper as follows:
vancomycin 125 mg four times a day for 14 days (___)
then 125 mg 2x/day for 7 days (___)
then 125  mg once a day for 7 days, (___)
then 125 mg once every two days for 8 days  (___) (FOUR 
DOSES)
then 125 mg once every three days for 15 days (___) 
(FIVE DOSES)

load undetectable but CD4 23 in ___. As verified with 
outpatient facility, he was on azithromycin and atovaquone 
prophylaxis. He was continued on all of these therapies during 
this admission. He also had his HIV viral load rechecked and it 
was undetectable.  CD$ count of 224.

microbiology.comments: HIV-1 RNA is not detected.  Performed using the ___ HIV-1 Test v2.0.  Detection Range: 20-10,000,000 copies/mL.  This test is approved for monitoring HIV-1 viral load in known HIV-positive patients. It is not approved for diagnosis of acute HIV infection.  In symptomatic acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), the viral load is usually very high (>>1000 copies/mL). If acute HIV infection is clinically suspected and there is a detectable but low viral load, please contact the laboratory for interpretation.  It is recommended that any NEW positive HIV-1 viral load result, in the absence of positive serology, be confirmed by submitting a new sample FOR HIV-1 PCR, in addition to serological testing.
